5. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the plaintiffs having failed to prove their settlement and having at no stage challenged the notification under section 4 of the Forest Act cannot raise objection regarding non-publication of notification under section 20 of the said Act and also the submission that the High Court Division was wrong in not taking into consideration that the alleged settlements of the plaintiffs are simply unauthorised for want of approval by the Chief Manager of the Bhawal Court of Wards Estate and those are fictitious and therefore, the plaintiffs possession in part of the suit plots is not lawful and the plaintiffs being trespassers cannot get a decree for permanent injunction and the further submission that the High Court Division ought to have held that a simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable when complicated question of title is involved and the plaintiffs have failed to prove their lawful possession. 

 The case of the plaintiffs is that, they took settlement of the suit plots from Bhawal Court of Wards Estate on 4-5-1949 on payment of salami and rent, etc by two salami receipts subject to the approval by the Chief Manager of the Estate. Photo copies of the salami receipts have been incorporated in the additional paper book filed by the appellant. From these salami receipts it appears that settlement was granted subject to approval by the Chief Manager of the Estate. But in the same receipt it was written on the same date that approval by the Chief Manager of the estate was duly accorded. This appears to be highly improbable. The plaintiffs also filed photo copies of Khatian No.B/412 of Mouza Araisha Proshad, PS Keraniganj, District-Dhaka to show that their names were duly mutated in the Khatian by order dated 16-10-1934 and on this date below the signature of the authorised officer the figure 34 is overwritten without any authentication. 

 17. We also do not find any cogent reason to disbelieve Exhibit-B, an agreement made on 22nd June, 1954 between one Jnan Chandra Dhar and the Government for sale of Gazari trees from the suit plots and other plots. The learned Additional Attorney-General next argued that since a complicated question of title is involved in the matter, a simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable and the courts below lost sight of this important aspect of the matter. The learned Additional Attorney-General has cited the case of Abu Musa vs Bangladesh reported in 2 BLC (AD) 56 and submitted in that case, it was held that since the salami receipts were not proved by the Chief Manager of the Estate, the High Court Division has rightly found that no lease was granted in favour of the plaintiffs. In this case it was further held that as the plaintiffs failed to prove their settlement and did not challenge the notification under section 4 of the Act, it does not lie in their mouth to complain that there was no final notification under section 20 of the Act. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submitted that the facts of the cited case are similar to the facts of the case before us and the principles of law enunciated in that case are fully applicable in the present case.
